(a) Static: research_library.py, workspace_library.py, library_ask.py and ocr_runtime.py import no network module. (a) OCR runs the bundled tesseract and tessdata via subprocess; ocr_runtime.py has no download code. A Library page render only calls ai_context.readiness, which reads the local settings and the OS credential store (CredReadW/keyring). It triggers no list_models, test_connection or update check. Backups and copies are local file I/O; the packaged self-test uses a local temp library.

(b) For all three adapters (OpenAI /v1/responses, Anthropic /v1/messages, Gemini :generateContent), I captured the request bytes on a loopback mock. Each body decodes to exactly request.prompt as the single user message, with no system or instructions field and no extra body keys. Headers are Content-Type, a constant User-Agent, the auth header, and anthropic-version for Anthropic; nothing is researcher-specific. Title and version attributes are sanitised and a '</source><source id=S9>' breakout is neutralised.

(b) send() rebuilds the request and compares it with what the last render previewed: the prompt (ticked passages, question, UI language) and (provider, model). On any difference it shows 'preview changed' and sends nothing (workspace_library.py:975-985). Question edits, which do not re-render, are caught this way. The exact preview text is shown unabridged (wc.text without max_lines). No keyboard shortcut triggers Send (workspace_shell.on_keyboard).

(c) A double click is safe: busy is set before the first await, so the second task returns. Cancel stops retries via cancel.wait; a late reply is dropped via the ticket and logged as 'cancelled'. A read timeout sends exactly one POST in the new path (the RC fix holds). Each new Send after an answer or error is a fresh click on a visible preview.

(d) The library prompt holds only the RULES, the answer language, and per passage its label, title, version, location and text, plus the question. It holds no data rows (the branch's PayloadTests plus the code), no results, no project name, no profile fields and no paths: the fallback title is Path(name).stem; a PDF /Title is used unless it looks like a file name. All of this is visible in the exact preview.

(e) The project activity log records provider, model, sources ['library'], tokens, outcome and task. The library's ai_transfers table records provider, model, sorted cite IDs, tokens and outcome. Cite IDs have the form D<sha256 prefix>-p<page>.<n> or -s<n>.<n> and contain no text. app.status messages are UI-only; nothing is written to Python logging.
Answer rendering uses plain ft.Text spans (no Markdown, no links) and offers only Copy and Discard, so an injected remote image or link cannot be fetched automatically.

(f) Correctly excluded: UUID text columns, unique text codes with digits (including when bulk-confirmed) and prose of 6 or more words bulk-confirmed as categories. Correctly kept: numeric Likert, short EN/LV/RU agreement labels and age. The preview (ai-preview-excluded) and Settings (ai-excluded-raw_data) name excluded columns in EN/LV/RU, and data_rows is 0 when nothing is left. The dictionary source sends only names and levels.

Backups: the library travels only through travelling_files, and only when backup.json says include_in_backups is true (off by default). The only copytree in project_store copies datasets and figures; nothing else carries library/.

Design note, not a finding: Ask with sources is gated by provider readiness plus a per-query preview and Send (library_ask.py:237 calls refusals with no sources), not by the per-project source permissions. The first three passages are pre-ticked, and the exact prompt sits in a collapsed tile. Library passages may themselves be transcripts.

findings.area: (d) hostile files - PDF content-stream bomb via pdfium
findings.claim: Pages without a text layer are probed with pdfium (_pdf_image_share). It inflates the page's whole content stream with no size cap and no cancel check. A few-MB PDF can exhaust memory, and pdfium then aborts the whole process with no message. A few-hundred-KB PDF whose many pages share one bomb stream keeps the worker busy for tens of minutes after Cancel.
findings.evidence: research_library.py:801-806 sends every page with fewer than 25 letters to _pdf_image_share (:652-676). That function loads each page's objects with pypdfium2, with no limit and no _check(cancel) in the loop. pypdf's 75 MB per-stream cap does not apply there. Measured with in-memory PDFs: a 1.5 MB PDF with one page inflating to 1.5 GB was accepted after 2.9 s, with peak RSS rising 92 -> 2,614 MB. A 4.0 MB PDF inflating to 4 GB under 'ulimit -v 3000000' killed the process with SIGABRT (exit 134) and no Python exception. Isolated: _pdf_lines (pypdf) on that page returned normally (exit 0), while _pdf_image_share(data, [1]) alone aborted (exit 134). This is consistent with PDFium terminating on allocation failure. Time: 8 pages sharing one 300 MB-inflating stream (300 KB file) took 5.5 s, and 32 pages took 21.3 s in pdfium (~0.67 s/page, linear, so ~22 min at MAX_PAGES=2000). With cancel set from the progress callback at ('read', n, n), extract still ran 21.5 s and returned normally; cancel is only checked later, in add_document at :1458. At MAX_BYTES = 64 MB, one stream can inflate to ~64 GB. render_pdf_page and ocr_page (:679-725) use pdfium the same way.

(b) ASCII, whitespace, case and newline variants of </source> and <source are rewritten to '< /source' / '< source'. The title, version and location attributes go through _attribute (quotes become ', <> become ‹›, whitespace collapsed, 160 chars), so there is no attribute or newline break-out. (c) At add time the stored copy is sha256 plus a whitelisted suffix. Path(name).name strips directories under Windows rules: '..\\..\\evil.pdf' -> 'evil.pdf', 'C:x.pdf' -> 'x.pdf', a UNC path -> 'p.docx'. CON.pdf and aux.pdf are stored as <sha256>.pdf. 'a.pdf.', 'a.pdf ', 'a.pdf:x' (ADS) and 'NUL' are refused as unsupported. A 300-char or RLO-containing name is only display text, duplicate names become v1/v2, and copies are written atomically and unlinked if indexing fails. Symlinks to regular files are read by content and stored by hash. Caveat, not reachable from the Windows picker: the size check uses stat().st_size, which is 0 for special files, so read_bytes() of e.g. a symlink to /dev/zero is not bounded by MAX_BYTES.

(d) PDF handling: a file with a user password gives 'encrypted'. Owner-password-only AES-256 and RC4-128 files (empty user password) are read, since cryptography 50.0.2 is locked. A bad startxref is recovered, and truncated or random-body PDFs give 'unreadable'. A 2.2 KB page tree with 10^6 leaves hits pypdf 6.21.4's limit (100,000 tree entries) and gives 'unreadable' in 0.87 s. pypdf's 75 MB per-stream cap holds for text extraction.

(d) DOCX handling: external entities (file:// and http://) are not resolved and nothing is fetched, because python-docx parses with resolve_entities=False (the leaked marker was absent). Billion-laughs is refused by lxml's amplification limit -> 'unreadable', and malformed XML -> 'unreadable'.

(d) TXT handling: cp1257, cp1251, UTF-16LE without BOM and 4 KB of random bytes all decode without exceptions (order: UTF-8, then a UTF-16 BOM, then cp1251/cp1257 with replacement). NUL and the snippet marks \x02/\x03 are removed by clean_text. There is no partial library: rows are written in one transaction, and the stored copy is unlinked on failure or cancel.

findings.area: tokenizer mirror vs unicode61 (fallback, 'Why this source?')
findings.claim: The Python mirror of unicode61 differs from FTS5 on private-use symbols and on combining marks NFC cannot compose. The fallback's scores and order diverge from FTS5 on such text, and on the default FTS5 backend 'Why this source?' contradicts the match.
findings.evidence:
Exhaustive per-code-point comparison, U+0080–U+2FFFF, remove_diacritics 2: 58,551 of 194,432 code points tokenize differently. Besides unassigned or newer-Unicode characters, this includes:
- all 6,400 BMP private-use characters, e.g. the U+F0B7 Symbol-font bullets in Word PDFs (an FTS5 token, a Python separator);
- 727 combining marks, which FTS5 keeps inside the token and strips while Python splits the word, e.g. Russian stress marks (U+0301);
- U+0130 İ → Python 'I' (upper case) vs FTS5 'i'.
Example: ' stress Моде́ль' → Python ['stress','моде','ль'] vs FTS5 ['','stress','модель'].
Effects:
- One PUA-bulleted passage changes avgdl, so every fallback score differs (0.39991 vs 0.394907) and the 'stress' order flips.
- The 'модель' order flips.
- 'тревожность студентов' finds 2 passages with FTS5 and 1 with the fallback.
- On the default FTS5 backend, explain() counts with Python tokens (research_library.py:1780, 1823-1836) and reports the rank-1 stress-marked passage as matched=() missing=('тревожнос…','студент…').
- query_terms does not NFC-normalise: decomposed 'vientulības' → ['vientul…','bas…'].
The claim at STAGE37_RAG.md:103-104 holds only for ordinary text: 3,012 random and 3,600 filtered queries gave 0 differences.

def test_python_tokens_equal_fts5_on_pdf_bullets_and_stress_marks(self):

        db.execute("CREATE VIRTUAL TABLE t USING fts5(a, tokenize='unicode61 remove_diacritics 2')")
        db.execute("CREATE VIRTUAL TABLE v USING fts5vocab(t, 'instance')")
